lessons.title: Common Greetings: Hello, Goodbye, Good Morning
lessons.body: In Arabic, greetings change depending on the time of day and formality. The most common hello is 'As-salaam alaykum' (peace be upon you), replied with 'Wa alaykum as-salaam'. For a simple hi, use 'Marhaba' or 'Ahlan'. Good morning is 'Sabah al-khayr' (morning of goodness), replied with 'Sabah an-nur' (morning of light). Good evening is 'Masa al-khayr', replied with 'Masa an-nur'. Goodbye is 'Ma'a as-salaama' (go with safety), replied with 'Allah yisallimak' or simply 'Ma'a as-salaama'. In Africa, especially in countries like Egypt, Sudan, and Morocco, you'll hear these daily. For example, in Cairo, a shopkeeper might greet you with 'Ahlan wa sahlan' (welcome). In Zanzibar, Swahili greetings mix with Arabic: 'Habari' is common, but Arabic 'Marhaba' is understood. Practice with a partner: greet at different times of day. Record yourself on your phone and compare to native audio on YouTube. Use apps like Duolingo or Memrise for repetition. Write each greeting on a flashcard with the English on the back. Review 5 minutes daily. In 3 days, you'll know 6 greetings. In 1 week, you can greet anyone in Arabic. Remember: in Africa, greetings are long and friendly. Don't rush. Ask about family, health, and work. 'As-salaam alaykum' opens doors. Try it with a neighbor from Sudan or Somalia. They'll smile and reply. That's your first real conversation.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself: Name, Origin, and Nationality
lessons.body: To introduce yourself in Arabic, start with 'Ismi' (my name is) followed by your name. For example, 'Ismi Amina' means 'My name is Amina'. To ask someone's name, say 'Ma ismuka?' (to a male) or 'Ma ismuki?' (to a female). To say where you are from, use 'Ana min' (I am from) plus your country. 'Ana min Nigeria' means 'I am from Nigeria'. For nationality, Arabic uses a suffix: 'Nigeriyy' (Nigerian male), 'Nigeriyya' (Nigerian female). Similarly, 'Misri' (Egyptian male), 'Misriyya' (Egyptian female). In Africa, you might say 'Ana min Kenya' (I am from Kenya) or 'Ana Sudani' (I am Sudanese). To ask 'Where are you from?' say 'Min ayna anta?' (male) or 'Min ayna anti?' (female). Practice with a friend: swap names, countries, and nationalities. Use a mirror to watch your mouth movements. Record a 30-second introduction on your phone. Listen for mistakes. Use online resources like ArabicPod101 or Forvo for pronunciation. Write your introduction in Arabic script and transliteration. For example: 'As-salaam alaykum. Ismi John. Ana min Ghana. Ana Ghanawi.' (Hello. My name is John. I am from Ghana. I am Ghanaian.) Repeat until fluent. In Africa, knowing how to introduce yourself in Arabic helps in business, travel, and making friends. In 2 days, you can introduce yourself confidently. Try it with a Arabic speaker in your community. They'll appreciate the effort.

lessons.title: Asking and Answering 'How Are You?'
lessons.body: The most common way to ask 'How are you?' in Arabic is 'Kayfa haluk?' (to a male) or 'Kayfa haluki?' (to a female). In Egyptian Arabic, you'll hear 'Izzayyak?' (male) and 'Izzayyik?' (female). In Levantine Arabic, it's 'Kifak?' (male) and 'Kifik?' (female). To answer, say 'Ana bi-khayr' (I am fine) or 'Al-hamdulillah' (Praise God). If you're not fine, say 'Ana mish bi-khayr' (I am not fine) or 'Ta'ban' (tired). In Africa, especially in Egypt, Sudan, and Morocco, these phrases are used daily. For example, in Cairo, a taxi driver might ask 'Izzayyak?' You reply 'Al-hamdulillah'. To ask 'How is your family?' say 'Kayfa hal al-usra?' or 'Izzayy al-ahil?' (Egyptian). Practice with a language partner on WhatsApp or Tandem. Set a goal: learn 3 ways to ask and 3 ways to answer. Use flashcards with audio. Listen to Arabic songs or news for intonation. Record yourself asking and answering. Compare to native speakers on YouTube. In 1 week, you can ask and answer 'How are you?' naturally. In Africa, this greeting shows respect and care. Don't just say 'fine' and walk away. Ask back: 'Wa anta?' (And you?). This builds rapport. Try it with a Sudanese friend. They'll be impressed.

lessons.title: Polite Expressions: Please, Thank You, Excuse Me
lessons.body: In Arabic, 'please' is 'Min fadlak' (to a male) or 'Min fadlik' (to a female). 'Thank you' is 'Shukran'. The response is 'Afwan' (you're welcome). 'Excuse me' is 'Afwan' as well, but for getting attention, say 'Law samaht' (if you please, male) or 'Law samahti' (female). For 'I'm sorry', say 'Asif' (male) or 'Asifa' (female). In Africa, these phrases are essential in markets, taxis, and offices. For example, in Morocco, when you want to pass, say 'Law samaht'. In Egypt, 'Shukran' is used constantly. To say 'Thank you very much', say 'Shukran jazeelan'. To say 'No, thank you', say 'La, shukran'. Practice with role-plays: buying bread, asking for directions, apologizing for being late. Use apps like HelloTalk to chat with native speakers. Write each phrase on a sticky note and place it where you'll see it. Repeat aloud 10 times. Record yourself. In 3 days, you'll use these naturally. In Africa, politeness opens doors. A simple 'Shukran' to a vendor can lead to a discount. 'Afwan' to a stranger who helps you. Try it today: say 'Shukran' to a Arabic-speaking colleague. They'll smile. Then say 'Min fadlak' when you ask for something. You'll be treated with respect.

lessons.title: Numbers 1-10 and Counting Basics
lessons.body: Arabic numbers 1-10 are: wahid (1), ithnan (2), thalatha (3), arba'a (4), khamsa (5), sitta (6), sab'a (7), thamaniya (8), tis'a (9), ashara (10). In Africa, these are used in Egypt, Sudan, Morocco, and other Arabic-speaking countries. To count objects, use the number plus the noun. For example, 'khamsa kutub' (five books). For 11-20, the pattern changes: ahada ashar (11), ithna ashar (12), etc. Practice counting from 1 to 10 aloud. Use your fingers. Write the numbers in Arabic script and transliteration. Use flashcards with the numeral on one side and the Arabic word on the other. Test yourself: say the number in Arabic when you see a digit. Use apps like Anki for spaced repetition. In 2 days, you'll know 1-10. In 1 week, you can count to 20. In daily life, use numbers for prices, phone numbers, and quantities. For example, in a Cairo market, ask 'Bikam?' (How much?) and the vendor says 'Khamsa junayh' (five pounds). You reply 'Shukran'. Practice with a friend: one says a number in English, the other in Arabic. Do this for 5 minutes daily. In Africa, bargaining is common. Knowing numbers helps you get fair prices. Try it at a local shop. Say 'Wahid, ithnan, thalatha' as you count items. The shopkeeper will notice.

lessons.title: Days of the Week and Months
lessons.body: In Arabic, days of the week are: al-ithnayn (Monday), ath-thulatha (Tuesday), al-arbi'a (Wednesday), al-khamis (Thursday), al-jum'a (Friday), as-sabt (Saturday), al-ahad (Sunday). Note that Friday is the holy day, and Sunday is 'the first'. Months in Arabic follow two systems: Gregorian and Islamic. Gregorian months are: Yanayir (January), Fibrayir (February), Maris (March), Abril (April), Mayu (May), Yunyu (June), Yulyu (July), Aghustus (August), Sibtambar (September), Oktubar (October), Nufambar (November), Disambar (December). Islamic months are: Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-awwal, Rabi' al-thani, Jumada al-ula, Jumada al-akhira, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qi'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah. In Africa, both are used. For example, in Egypt, Ramadan is a key month. In Morocco, Gregorian months are common in business. Practice saying the days in order. Use a calendar and point to each day. Write the Arabic name next to the English. Use songs or rhymes to memorize. For months, learn the Gregorian first, then Islamic. In 3 days, you'll know the days. In 1 week, the months. Use them in sentences: 'Al-yawm al-ithnayn' (Today is Monday). 'Shahru Ramadan' (the month of Ramadan). In Africa, knowing days and months helps with appointments, holidays, and business. Try scheduling a meeting in Arabic: 'Al-jum'a, min fadlak' (Friday, please).

quiz.q: What is the most common Arabic greeting meaning 'peace be upon you'?
quiz.explanation: 'As-salaam alaykum' is the standard Islamic greeting used across Arabic-speaking Africa.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Good morning' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: 'Sabah al-khayr' means 'morning of goodness' and is used in the morning.

quiz.q: What is the reply to 'Sabah al-khayr'?
quiz.explanation: 'Sabah an-nur' (morning of light) is the traditional response.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Goodbye' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: 'Ma'a as-salaama' means 'go with safety' and is used when parting.

quiz.q: What does 'Ahlan wa sahlan' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ahlan wa sahlan' is a warm welcome used in many African countries.

quiz.q: How do you say 'My name is Amina' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: 'Ismi' means 'my name is', followed by the name.

quiz.q: What is the question 'Where are you from?' for a male?
quiz.explanation: 'Min ayna anta?' is used for a male; 'anti' for female.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am from Nigeria' for a male?
quiz.explanation: 'Ana min' means 'I am from', followed by the country.

quiz.q: What is the nationality word for a Nigerian female?
quiz.explanation: The suffix '-iyya' is added for feminine nationality adjectives.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What is your name?' to a female?
quiz.explanation: 'Ma ismuki?' is used for a female; 'ismuka' for male.

quiz.q: What is the common way to ask 'How are you?' in Modern Standard Arabic to a male?
quiz.explanation: 'Kayfa haluk?' is the standard masculine form.

quiz.q: What does 'Al-hamdulillah' mean in response to 'How are you?'
options: B) I am fine, praise God
quiz.explanation: 'Al-hamdulillah' is a common positive reply meaning 'Praise God'.

quiz.q: In Egyptian Arabic, how do you ask 'How are you?' to a female?
quiz.explanation: 'Izzayyik?' is the Egyptian feminine form.

quiz.q: What is the reply to 'Kayfa haluk?' meaning 'I am fine'?
quiz.explanation: 'Ana bi-khayr' means 'I am fine'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'And you?' to a male after being asked 'How are you?'
quiz.explanation: 'Wa anta?' means 'And you?' to a male.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic word for 'please' to a male?
quiz.explanation: 'Min fadlak' is used when addressing a male.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Thank you' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: 'Shukran' means 'thank you'.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Shukran'?
quiz.explanation: 'Afwan' means 'you're welcome'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Excuse me' to get attention from a male?
quiz.explanation: 'Law samaht' is used for a male; 'samahti' for female.

quiz.q: What does 'Asif' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Asif' means 'I'm sorry' for a male.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic number for 5?
quiz.explanation: 'Khamsa' is the number 5.

quiz.q: How do you say 'three' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: 'Thalatha' is the number 3.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic number for 10?
quiz.explanation: 'Ashara' is the number 10.

quiz.q: How do you say 'five books' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: The number precedes the noun: 'khamsa kutub'.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic number for 7?
quiz.explanation: 'Sab'a' is the number 7.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic word for Monday?
quiz.explanation: 'Al-ithnayn' means Monday.

quiz.q: Which day is 'al-jum'a'?
quiz.explanation: 'Al-jum'a' is Friday, the holy day.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic name for January?
quiz.explanation: 'Yanayir' is January in the Gregorian calendar.

quiz.q: Which Islamic month is the month of fasting?
quiz.explanation: 'Ramadan' is the month of fasting.

quiz.q: What is the Arabic word for Sunday?
quiz.explanation: 'Al-ahad' means Sunday (the first day).
